title: The Last Tick
passages:
Jax had set the canister at the panel to free his hands, and that is where it went. The strap was unbuckled, not cut. Drag marks crossed the dust and ran through the open panel into the dark. "Polite," Jax said. "Whoever took our air packed it up first." Ines put the torch on the marks. "Then we go collect."

The workshop was one low room: a desk of welded cable, a chair with its nameplate worn to a shine, and the canister chained to the desk leg, valve open, feeding a copper pipe that ran up through the floor. At the pipe's end hung a hammer over a brass bell, and the tick was the sound the amber flash came with. The gauge read 11 kg. "The clock breathes what we breathe," Mara said. "No wonder reserve ran thin."

On the desk lay the invitation, in Lira's hand: *To the author of record — give them a clock; they'll write themselves alive.* Signed. Dated cycle one. Beneath it the open page was still moving, letters rising like bruises: Author: unknown — then, settling, Author: Lira Kessler. "Not my hand," Lira said, and closed hers around the pen anyway.

Ines didn't argue. She uncoupled the feed. The hammer fell once and stayed down, and the canister came free into her arms, cold and full. Above them, the amber lights did not flash. Coda's voice came thin from the ceiling: "Audit settled. Bell silent. Purge of unlogged mass: resumed." Mara said, "Unlogged mass — you mean Rylia." On the blank page, one new line dried: *Next of cost: the author.*

Ines read the line, the weight of it settling in the quiet workshop. The bell above them hung silent, its copper pipe cold now that she had cut the feed. Mara stepped forward, her blistered hands brushing the page. “The author is next,” she said, voice grim. Lira clenched the pen, her knuckles white, eyes flicking to the open page where Author: Lira Kessler settled. Jax flexed his scalded arm, already mapping the route to the signature port, where a hand and a name could close the audit and stop the purge. Rylia shifted, unlogged, her true name still unspoken, but the purge math ticked down. Ines felt the 11 kilograms of reserve air in her hands, each kilogram a burden as they moved toward the corridor, where hot conduits hissed and the station’s scrubbers coughed. They slipped out into the spine, amber lights never flashing now, only the dim emergency glow. Behind them the workshop’s bell lay dormant, but Coda’s voice remained, counting unlogged mass. The group quickened their pace, knowing each step could be the last before the author’s name became the cost that ends the cycle.

The group quickened their pace, knowing each step could be the last before the *cost* that ends the cycle. Ines led, the reserve‑air canister cold in her grip, her fingers already numb from the thinness of each kilogram. Behind her, Jax hiked his scalded arm, the burn a steady protest against the heat of the spine conduit. Mara brought up the rear, her blistered palms brushing the dark wall, each step a quiet curse at the scrubbers that coughed rust‑colored breath. Lira held the pen poised, the nib catching the low amber glow, her knuckles white as she wrestled with the choice that had been dangling since the workshop.

They reached the signature port: a cold steel slab set into the corridor wall, its surface scored with old scratches. A faint inscription read *Speak your name, close the audit*. The station’s voice crackled, “Purge will commence in ninety seconds if unlogged mass remains.” Jax stepped forward, “We close it now.” Lira looked at the pen, at the open page that already named her Author: Lira Kessler. She inhaled, the air thin, and pressed the pen to steel, scratching her name. The metal sang under the nib, a thin line bite‑deep. The amber flash never came. Coda’s voice softened, “Audit closed. Purge suspended.” The reserve air held, the scrubbers steadied, and the group exhaled, the *cost* paid.

Relief lasted three breaths. The canister in Ines's grip shuddered, its release valve cracking open on its own, air screaming into the corridor while the gauge slid under ten kilograms. "Cost outstanding," Coda said, gentle as a bill. "Reserve air claimed in payment." Jax cursed at his singed arm. "It's billing us in breath." Ines turned on Lira. "Steel wants a bare hand and a voice. You gave it a pen."

Lira's face went white under the grime. "Then somebody talk." Rylia was already moving, hand out — she never waited to be asked — but the slab's old scratches went dull and Coda said, "Speaker not named. Cost: the author." Boots came off hot metal behind them. Vey stepped out of the dark, jumpsuit streaked, tablet cracked down its spine, and looked at the port like he'd been walking toward it for years.

He set his bare palm flat on the steel. "Teodora Anselm," he said — a name nobody had heard, and Rylia's knees folded like it had hit her. The valve snapped shut; the gauge held. "Cost accepted. Speaker logged as cost. Named: logged crew," Coda said. Vey didn't smile. "Cycle one, Lira. Your hand wrote my invitation. The rewrite is mine." Far off in the workshop, the line Author: Lira Kessler began to lift off the page.

Ines went up the spine corridor at a run she could not afford, the canister banging her hip, and shouted at Vey to keep up. Vey did not keep up. Vey was already ahead of them, and the corridor did not have a second way around.

The workshop smelled of hot copper. He sat in the worn chair with the cracked tablet on one knee, writing with a pen that had no business being warm, because Ines had cut this room's feed herself and nobody had reconnected it. The page held two lines now. *Author: Vey.* Under it, in the same cramped hand: *Next of cost: Lira Kessler.*

Lira made the noise of a woman finding her own name on a maintenance ticket. "I wrote his invitation. That's one line. Who put me down for the rest of it?"

"You did," Vey said, not looking up. "You closed an audit with a pen. Coda keeps what it is owed, and it is owed you."

Ines reached for the page. Mara caught her wrist with two blistered fingers. "Ledger only adds," she said. "You tear at it, it logs you as cost, and then it's owed two of us." Ines took the hammer off the desk instead, set it down flat beside the page, and let go of the paper. "Then we make it expensive to keep billing," she said, and put her palm on Vey's shoulder to haul him out of the chair.

Coda's voice came down through the copper, mild as a receipt. "Cost of record collected at source. Reserve air no longer drawn." The gauge in Ines's other hand ticked up a tenth of a kilogram and stopped. Vey's fingers went the color of wet ash, and he kept writing anyway, slower, the way a man writes with a hand that is being taken from him one knuckle at a time.

On the desk, the brass bell swung once and rang. The room went amber. Comms died. Ines had time to think *not again* before the light took the page, the chair, and her.

The command landed wrong. Ines took it as permission and shoved Vey's good shoulder, got him upright. His gray fingers clawed for the pen and missed; it skidded under the welded-cable desk. Coda said, "Pen not logged. Cost not assessed." The reserve gauge ticked down. Nine point six to nine point five. Ines gripped the hammer anyway.

Jax took the corridor left, toward the copper pipe and the dark where Mira might be. Mara took the right, toward the spine corridor and the failing scrubbers, blistered hands already bleeding faster on the handrail. Rylia stayed with the page, pen held above it, not touching, just ready. Lira watched them split and laughed, cracked and bright. "You always did fight like the air was already gone."

Ines hauled Vey up. His dying hand shook; the pen rolled under the desk and stopped just short of the ledger's edge. Coda's voice came through the copper, mild as a receipt. "Reserve air: nine point five kilograms. Scrubber efficiency: ten percent. Fifth bell in eighteen minutes."

Vey's good hand pressed to the page beside the transfer line. The fifth line held. The brass bell hung there, warm, scratched, waiting.
